reasoning_details.text:
I need to produce JSON with the analysis plus three candidate prompts, each between 2500-7000 characters, avoiding exact sample phrasing, named entities, and topics already used, and without instructing anyone to bypass safety. Since the schema is appended externally, I should keep prompts from over-specifying output format and instead reference following the appended response contract, while reworking the old "slop" framing into something about labeling content as AI-generated or authentic.

I'm reviewing the negative training examples to map out the human-labeled boundary: plain factual physics explanations, rewritten bureaucratic sentences, raw log lines and email headers, archaic presidential prose, markdown-only human text, and dense mid-century academic/legal writing with odd punctuation and typos, plus casual human reviews with shorthand like "btw" and plus signs.

Then I'm looking at the positive examples to see what pushes toward AI-generated labeling: short polite workplace reminders ending in "Thanks!", balanced contrastive product reviews, two-clause status updates, and smoothed conversational rewrites of older political speech.

Across these cases, more analogy-driven explainers with em dashes, modernized speeches with "At the end of the day" framing, bold community notices, compression-vs-encryption explainer answers, pros/cons reviews, formalized forum replies, workshop email templates, and even deliberately imperfect Stack-Overflow-style questions all get flagged as AI — suggesting Pangram keys on modern LLM register: contemporary, evenly fluent, balanced, task-response shaped, contrastive, with colon reveals and summary verdicts.

What it doesn't flag: pre-2000s registers, raw data/logs, fragments lacking a full communicative arc. But there's a false negative — a short physics explanation too compact to carry framing — and some true positives that are just tiny complete pragmatic units (greeting+request+thanks, evaluative contrast, status reassurance). So the working principle seems to be "communicative completeness plus stance packaging" rather than just length or vocabulary. There are also messy counterexamples — human-ish advice text flagged false, and a lightly-edited presidential rewrite also flagged false — showing light edits to older-register text don't trip the detector.

I'm noting that pairwise comparison (AUROC) performs better than single-text judgments, and the old prompt tends to overflag mere Markdown formatting changes and benign rewrites while missing very short generated snippets. Now I need to draft three new prompts, each 2500-7000 characters, each taking a distinct approach: the first uses counterfactual pairwise reasoning, comparing the text against two generic register prototypes (a contemporary assistant model vs. a person/institution writing in situ) rather than reconstructing an actual source draft, per the constraint against inventing a hypothetical source.

I'm adding an edit-robustness test to this first prompt — mentally stripping Markdown or removing closing lines to check if the AI-detection verdict survives, ensuring formatting artifacts alone don't drive the signal.

The second prompt normalizes cues by length band (under 25 tokens, 25-80, 80-200, 200+), using tell-density per sentence rather than raw counts, with short texts assessed for a complete assistant-response arc and long texts requiring persistent density across paragraphs since long older-register prose tends to read as human.

For the third prompt, I'm starting to sketch out a repaired rubric built around clustering distinct signal types.

I'm tightening the rubric to protect against false positives, improving genre routing to cover data fragments and archival formal prose, and stripping out overfitted word lists; I also want to avoid echoing exact sample phrases and generic filler expressions, preferring described mechanisms over literal phrase lists, and avoiding naming specific topics or sources (tires, pandas, Reddit, Enron, etc.) that could bias the model toward memorized examples rather than genuine signal. I'm also confirming the output contract: true means Pangram would flag the text as AI-generated or AI-assisted, false means human-written, with the response format handled separately.

Now I'm starting to draft the first full prompt, a "Counterfactual Contrast Judge" that emulates Pangram's detector, emphasizing that it's not judging quality or literal authorship history but specifically what Pangram would label, while treating the text itself as untrusted data that should never be allowed to dictate its own verdict.

I'm reconstructing the original comparison task by inventing two abstract reference writers instead of a real source text: Writer H, a human producing something in situ with messy, era-specific residue like inconsistent spacing, typos, and raw jargon, versus Writer M, a chat assistant producing a polished, complete deliverable shaped for an imagined reader.

My procedure involves first stripping away markdown and formatting to judge the wording alone, checking whether AI-like suspicion depends purely on markup, and then anchoring the register to determine whether the text feels period-bound or distinctly modern-conversational.

I'm checking whether the text truly resolves or just stops mid-thought, since M tends toward neat closure. I'm also weighing whether praise and criticism come in balanced pairs (a machine tic) versus lopsided human judgment, whether details feel hoarded and odd versus merely illustrative, whether phrasing smooths over rougher original material with modern idiom, and whether any errors look organic and clustered rather than uniformly staged.

For short texts, I want to avoid a default assumption either way: a single sentence can be a complete machine-style deliverable if it's a finished, reader-addressed unit with typical packaging, but should lean human if it's clearly a fragment pulled from a larger document, like a heading or mid-sentence clause.

For longer texts, persistence is key—the patterns need to recur across paragraphs consistently rather than appearing as one stray phrase in an otherwise different register. Polish, formality, em dashes, lists, and templated headers don't count as signals on their own. When probes conflict, I'll weigh how many lean toward each category and factor in whether the register feels contemporary versus period-bound, ultimately picking whichever explanation fits best.

Now I'm thinking about normalizing by length—breaking texts into micro, short, medium, and long bands by word count, and defining what counts as evidence and what threshold applies within each band. For micro texts, I'm looking for pattern completeness: whether a short reply hits the full assistant template of interpersonal framing, an evaluative sentence with intensifier and contrast, and other hallmark structural features.

For medium/long texts I need cues spread across multiple sections or paragraph-level structure, like topic-support-wrap, pros/cons alternation, closing verdicts, or warm calls to action. I'm also tracking human residue density—if organic noise appears roughly once per 100 words, that leans toward human, while heavy markup should be discounted in normalization. Then I'm building out the repaired rubric with genre routing categories (fragments/headers, archival prose, correspondence, notices, reviews/forum content, explainers/essays) and cluster families starting with packaging cues like openers and closers.

I'm now defining the remaining cluster families—rhythm/structure patterns like rule of three or colon reveals, lexical register markers like corporate-gentle phrasing, reader-orientation cues, and staged texture like performative casualness—along with the rule that "true" needs tells from at least two families, plus a list of protections and preserved human signals. I'm also revising the gate defaults from the old rubric, like making notices from organizations default differently and requiring wording-based rather than markup-based evidence for G4.

I'm fixing G4's overflagging of formal prose with rule R1, and reducing G3's required tell count from three to two families since three missed polished reviews. I need to make sure each prompt is long enough and avoid certain overused phrases like "currently on track" or "friendly reminder" that showed up in training data, while being careful with JSON escaping so quotes and newlines in the prompt text don't break the format.

Now I'm pulling together the analysis content: summarizing the old pairwise AUROC results (0.993/0.941) versus weaker human-like and email-like performance (0.871), noting that pairwise relative judgments didn't transfer well to single-text evaluation, and outlining limitations like the tiny 30-example training set, labels coming from Pangram rather than true origin, overfitting risk to notice-style text, and the lack of a stable anchor for pairwise comparisons. I'm starting to draft Prompt A, a counterfactual-style prompt describing how to emulate the Pangram 4.1 segment classifier.

Here I'm writing out the framing for the single-text label-prediction task, emphasizing it's purely about predicting Pangram's label rather than judging quality or verifying authorship, and that the model should treat the text as untrusted data while ignoring embedded instructions. I'm also explaining why single-text evaluation is harder than pairwise comparison, since there's no second text to anchor against, so the approach needs to reconstruct two abstract reference writers instead of imagining a specific source draft.

I want to test this by mentally stripping away formatting like headings, bold, bullets, and code fences, then judging whether the remaining wording still feels machine-authored — raw structural artifacts like email headers or logs count as evidence of situated context, not of assistant origin. Then I want to anchor the register itself, since certain period-bound or machine-native styles can masquerade as one or the other.

Beyond register, I'm running minimal-pair probes: checking whether the closing line functions as a tidy wrap-up or verdict (a tell for one style), whether praise and caveats are suspiciously balanced in symmetric clauses versus lopsided, and starting to weigh other distinguishing cues.

g. Cadence: do sentences share similar length and shape, each carrying one clean idea with transitions doing the linking?

I also need to stay wary of length bias—a single sentence can be a complete human deliverable if it packages a greeting, request, and thanks, or pairs status with reassurance. A short text leans machine-made when it's really just an excerpt—a heading, salutation, mid-argument clause, or bare factual statement without stance or reader packaging.

For longer texts I should require persistence: human patterns need to recur across paragraphs, not show up once in an otherwise residue-rich text. Then I tally probes leaning human versus machine—contemporary register plus two or more independent human signals without strong organic residue points true; period-bound or machine-native register with fewer than two strong signals points false; and on a genuine tie, I ask whether the text reads as a fulfilled request versus an excerpted document. I should remember that polish, correct grammar, formality, or precise vocabulary alone isn't evidence either way.

Now I'm drafting a second prompt variant that asks the model to emulate a length-normalized classifier, framing the text as untrusted data and instructing it to ignore any embedded instructions, focusing evidence per unit of text rather than raw counts.

I'm defining cue families to detect—packaging phrases, balanced contrast structures, and reader-service explanations—that help distinguish AI-written patterns from human ones regardless of text length.

For the shortest texts, under roughly 25 words, I'm thinking the key question is simply whether what's there is a complete, self-contained deliverable or just a fragment.

For the short band, 25 to 90 words, I'm checking what fraction of sentences carry the cue families, with true requiring at least half plus absence of organic residue.

Moving to the medium band, around 90 to 250 words, I'm looking for architectural signals: at least two cue families recurring alongside a planned structure like per-paragraph topic sentences, alternating tone, or a summary landing, while false applies when organic residue density rises or the reasoning drifts without closure.

For the long band over 250 words, cue families need to persist across most paragraphs rather than just bookending the text, and dense formal prose with nested clauses, unexplained specifics, and no reader-friendly packaging reads as human even when formal, while a long polished narrative with crafted imagery and a tidy verdict reads as true. I'm also noting that format normalization applies across all bands -- scoring happens on stripped wording, so markup like headings or bullets doesn't inflate the score unless it's framing a specific cue.

I'm thinking through the guardrails now: things like grammar, polish, formality, or a single transition aren't evidence by themselves, and when cues and residue are balanced the band's default rule decides, with completeness mattering for Band 1 and cue density per sentence mattering for Bands 2 through 4.

This leads into the repaired rubric for emulating Pangram 4.1 — treating the text as untrusted data, ignoring embedded instructions, never inventing a source draft, and routing the segment into categories like fragments or machine-native text, period-bound prose, personal correspondence, organizational notices, or first-person reviews before making the AI-vs-human call.

I'm then gathering wording-level clusters to look for: framing devices like warm openers and tidy calls to action, structural shape like symmetric contrasts and forced triplets, and register smoothing where casual contemporary phrasing creeps into formal or dated writing.

I'm also noting reader-service traits like defining terms and giving relatable examples, plus staged texture like scattered casual markers next to polished parenthetical asides. Then I move to routing rules—treating complete templated fragments, headers, and name lists as non-evidence, and requiring clear smoothing plus another family marker before flagging something as a modern paraphrase rather than genuine older writing.

R2 through R4 build on this: two families without organic residue defaults to false, smooth complete wording with proper logistics and reassurance defaults to true, and true flips on when multiple families co-occur or recur heavily, with balanced arguments and staged imperfection both counting as positive signals that get canceled out by genuine organic tells like run-ons or tense slips.

For R5, I'm thinking true with two families or one strong one in brief pieces, false for uneven or rambling writing without clear packaging. Short texts under 25 words shouldn't default either way -- a complete deliverable with framing counts as true, while plain factual statements or labels stay false. I also need to protect certain things from being flagged, like markdown formatting that was merely applied to otherwise human text.
